title: TV Moments That Changed The World
summary: Hosts open the first episode of 2026 (a year-end style top-list episode, though not a numbered ten) with banter about TV's cultural impact. They cover the April 30, 1939 NBC broadcast of Franklin Roosevelt opening the New York World's Fair, Disney's Wonderful World of Color and the 1961 color TV debut, the first legal TV commercial (Bulova, July 1, 1941) and its Super Bowl cost comparison, media coverage driving charitable giving after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, Vietnam War television coverage and its effect on public opinion, the debut of Cops on Fox in 1989 and its racial stereotyping criticism, and the 1980 "Miracle on Ice" US hockey upset of the Soviet Union at Lake Placid. Closes with a note on the back catalog, tour dates, and a skipped listener mail segment.
topics: tsunami media coverage and charitable giving
Stuff You Should Know back catalog

segments.title: Opening and New Year banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the first episode of 2026, joke about the date and a year-end top list format, and tease the theme of TV's impact on modern culture.

segments.title: 1939 World's Fair TV broadcast
segments.summary: On April 30, 1939, NBC broadcast Franklin Roosevelt opening the New York World's Fair in Flushing, Long Island, reaching about two thousand viewers via mobile broadcast trucks. RCA sold luxury TVs and a transparent TV was shown at the RCA pavilion.

segments.title: Disney's Wonderful World of Color and color TV
segments.summary: Walt Disney pushed NBC to broadcast his anthology show in color. The first episode, Adventure in Color, aired September 24, 1961, with the Spectrum Song and Professor Ludwig von Drake. Hosts say the show helped drive color TV sales.

segments.title: Bulova: first TV commercial
segments.summary: On July 1, 1941, a Bulova clock-face ad ran for about nine to ten seconds during a Dodgers versus Phillies broadcast, costing nine dollars and widely considered the first legal TV commercial. Earlier sponsorship spots such as the Fox Furriers ad were not true commercials, and the FCC began issuing commercial licenses in 1941. The hosts compare the cost to a Super Bowl spot and then discuss the show's back catalog and how to find episodes.

segments.title: Back catalog and episode discovery
segments.summary: Hosts note the show has roughly 2,300 episodes including Short Stuff and discuss how listeners can find older episodes through podcast apps and the website search.

segments.title: Super Bowl ad cost comparison
segments.summary: The hosts note that a Bulova spot in the 2025 Super Bowl would have cost about two point three five million dollars for ten seconds.

segments.title: 2004 tsunami and media-driven giving
segments.summary: The December 26, 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, triggered by a roughly 9.0 undersea earthquake, killed close to 230,000 people. Round-the-clock media coverage drove large charitable giving, with a study finding one extra minute of TV coverage increased internet donations by a notable percentage and ninety-nine countries donating.

segments.title: Vietnam War television coverage
segments.summary: Handheld cameras let TV reporters reach the front lines in Vietnam, unlike the government-curated newsreels of WWII and Korea. With nearly all American homes owning a TV, broadcasts showed unflinching footage that shaped public opinion and likely pushed an earlier withdrawal. Later wars such as the Gulf War and Iraq War were covered differently, with embedded reporting and a 'shock and awe' framing.

segments.title: Cops and reality TV
segments.summary: Cops debuted on Fox on March 11, 1989, and is considered a precursor to reality TV, with no script or star. Hosts say it reinforced racial stereotypes; a 1994 Marshall Project analysis found sexual assault, robbery and murder were overrepresented relative to actual crime, and Black and brown suspects were associated with violent crime more often. Fox dropped the show in 2013 after pressure from Color of Change; it later ran on Spike TV and Fox Nation, and helped popularize the Florida Man stereotype.

segments.title: Miracle on Ice, 1980 Olympics
segments.summary: The US men's hockey team, coached by Herb Brooks and made up of college players, beat the Soviet Union 4-3 at the 1980 Lake Placid Winter Olympics after losing an exhibition 10-3. Al Michaels's 'Do you believe in miracles?' call became iconic. The hosts note the US went on to win gold against Finland two days later, and that the Soviet match was a medal-round game, not the gold medal game.

segments.title: Wrap-up of TV moments
segments.summary: Hosts conclude the list of TV moments that changed the world.
